one_liner: Rust reimplementation of the jq language and CLI; faster than jq 1.8.1 on 23 of 30 author filter benchmarks.
what_it_does: jaq is a clone of jq: the `jaq` binary is meant as a drop-in replacement for the `jq` command, and the jaq-core/jaq-std/jaq-json crates parse, compile and run jq filters inside Rust programs over any value type implementing the ValT trait. It also reads and writes YAML, CBOR, TOML, XML and XJON (JSON extended with byte strings and non-string object keys). Its semantics follow jq in most cases but differ in documented edge cases.
how_it_is_fast: Values are reference counted (arrays as Rc<Vec>, objects as Rc<IndexMap> hashed with foldhash) and updates go through Rc::make_mut copy-on-write, so an accumulator that is uniquely owned is mutated in place; that is why `reduce range(.) as $x ([[]]; .[0] += [$x])` finishes in under 10 ms where jq takes 720 ms. The compiler detects tail-recursive calls and executes them as tail-call exceptions that reuse the stack (tail-call optimisation in compile.rs and filter.rs), so recursive generators like `upto` run in under 10 ms versus 440 ms in jq. Filters run as lazy Rust iterators, numbers stay native isize integers (BigInt on overflow) or f64, with decimal literals kept as strings until used, and the CLI uses mimalloc by default.
when_to_use: jq programs that build or reshape large arrays and objects: sort of 1,048,576 numbers 90 ms vs 430 ms in jq, group_by 260 vs 1790 ms, reverse 30 vs 440 ms, kv-update 130 vs 440 ms.

Accumulating reduce/update loops and deep recursion in jq code (reduce-update, upto, Brainfuck interpreter bf-fib 530 vs 1030 ms), where copy-on-write and tail-call optimisation change the complexity.
Field extraction over multi-GB NDJSON: a third-party README (6/qj, M5 Max) lists jaq at 6.7 s vs jq 18.0 s and gojq 17.2 s for `.actor.login` on 3.4 GB (not verified here).
Embedding jq filters in a Rust service: jaq-core is no_std with alloc, forbids unsafe code, and accepts custom value types through ValT.
Running jq syntax over YAML, CBOR, TOML or XML without a separate conversion step.
when_not_to_use: Scripts that depend on exact jq behaviour: jaq errors on float array indices and on updating null with an index, returns nan/infinite for division by zero, prints NaN as NaN, treats `. |= empty` and multi-output reduce/foreach differently, slurps multiple files into one array per file, and lacks the `?//` operator.
Pipelines that need jq's --stream, --stream-errors, --seq, --ascii-output, --unbuffered or --jsonargs options, which jaq does not support.
Startup-bound use (many tiny invocations): 512 empty runs took 410 ms vs 430 ms for jq 1.8.1 and 270 ms for gojq; jaq's original startup edge was over jq 1.6.
Workloads shaped like the 7 rows jq won: reduce (700 vs 740 ms), try-catch, pyramid, tree-flatten (330 vs 700 ms; gojq 10 ms because it implements flatten natively), ack, range-prop, cumsum-xy.
Untrusted filters or inputs: the README states jaq takes no countermeasures against resource exhaustion, so deeply nested input or unbounded recursion can overflow the stack or exhaust memory.

integration.dependencies: jaq-core: dyn-clone, once_cell, typed-arena; jaq-json: indexmap, foldhash, num-bigint; CLI binary: mimalloc (default feature), rustyline, env_logger, log, dirs, tempfile
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.70 for the jaq CLI, Rust 1.69 for jaq-core (rust-version fields)
integration.platforms: any Rust target per the README; release binaries for Linux (musl), macOS and Windows; jaq-core is no_std plus alloc
integration.thread_safety: README says jaq-core can be used safely in multi-threaded environments, unlike the jq C API; jaq-json values are built on Rc (non-atomic), so each value stays in one thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the README calls the CLI a drop-in replacement for jq, but the manual's compatibility blocks list semantic divergences and six unsupported jq options

gotchas: Harness limits in bench.sh: it records only user CPU time (/usr/bin/time -f %U, 10 ms resolution), so system time is excluded. In issue #136 an earlier jaq lost to jq partly on system time (3.5 s vs 0.6 s, unbuffered stdout). The two 0 ms rows mean under 10 ms, so their ratios have no upper bound, and 7 of the 30 jaq-vs-jq rows differ by 10% or less (10 to 40 ms).
Each filter gets a single number as input and pipes its output through `| length`, so apart from to-fromjson the suite measures interpreter work, not parsing or printing large JSON documents.

del(.key) on an object swap-removes the entry (IndexMap swap_remove in jaq-json), so the last key moves into the deleted slot; open issue #436 reports `del(.b)` on {a,b,c,d} yielding {a,d,c}, while jq keeps the order.
The table measured jaq 3.0, while crates.io is at 3.1.1 (2026-08-05). The README's command line names gojq-0.12.17 while the table and footnote say 0.12.18.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick jaq when the work is running jq filter logic (sorting, grouping, updates, recursion) rather than raw parsing; for parse/serialise throughput inside C++ or Rust code, simdjson, yyjson or sonic-rs are the right tools. jist's numbers cover a single lookup on multi-GB files, whereas jaq implements the whole jq language.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran jaq 3.0 (cargo release build, codegen-units = 1) against jq 1.8.1 (Arch Linux package) and gojq 0.12.18 on 30 jq-filter benchmarks on a Linux AMD Ryzen 5 5500U laptop, taking the minimum user CPU time of 3 runs. jaq beat jq on 23 rows and lost on 7, e.g. sort 90 vs 430 ms and group_by 260 vs 1790 ms on 1,048,576 elements, and to/fromjson 50 vs 350 ms; jq won reduce 700 vs 740 ms and tree-flatten 330 vs 700 ms.
status_note: Actively maintained (commits through 2026-10-02, jaq 3.1.1 on crates.io with about 123k downloads), MIT-licensed; NLnet funded two security audits whose findings were fixed, and fuzz targets were added. Usable as a CLI or crate, with documented jq incompatibilities.
